advantages-school-international.challenge: Reporting on student progress reached families only at fixed points in the year, by which time any intervention was late.
advantages-school-international.solution: Embedded per-student dashboards in the parent portal, alongside internal cohort reporting for teaching staff.
advantages-school-international.results: Families see progress as it happens, and staff identify attendance and assessment drop-off within the week rather than the term.
advantages-school-international.body:
## Why live reporting

A periodic report summarises something that has already finished. For a student whose engagement slipped weeks ago, it arrives long after a conversation would have helped.

## What changed

Parents see attendance, assessment and submitted work for their own children, strictly scoped. Staff see the same data in aggregate with cohort comparison.

alto.challenge: The existing analytics stack was expensive, slow to work with, and unpopular enough that teams avoided it.
alto.solution: A web-first, container-friendly deployment alongside the existing infrastructure, with dashboards teams could build themselves.
alto.results: Platform cost fell sharply and usage spread well beyond the data team.
alto.body:
## Why they moved

The previous tool required local installation, did not fit the deployment model, and had low satisfaction across the company.

## What the data team does now

Departments manage their own collections. The data team maintains the models underneath rather than fielding requests.

angellist.challenge: Data access was concentrated in a small group, so most questions arrived as requests rather than being answered directly.
angellist.solution: Self-service analytics over modelled data, opened to every team rather than rationed.
angellist.results: People across the business explore data directly, and the data team moved from answering questions to maintaining the foundations.
angellist.body:
## The bottleneck

When only a few people can query, every question becomes a ticket and the queue defines the team's week.

## What helped

Modelling first. Agreeing definitions before opening access meant self-service produced consistent answers rather than contradictory ones.

aula.challenge: Customers asked repeatedly for reporting on engagement, and each request arrived as a support ticket.
aula.solution: Embedded analytics inside the learning platform, scoped per institution.
aula.results: Support tickets fell substantially once customers could answer their own questions.
aula.body:
## Support load as a signal

A recurring question in a support queue is usually a missing feature. Reporting requests were the clearest example.

## The approach

One embedded dashboard, filtered per institution, rather than bespoke reports per customer.

axway.challenge: Banking clients required analytics inside the product, running in environments with no outbound network access.
axway.solution: White-labelled embedded analytics deployed air-gapped, with dashboards shipped as part of the product.
axway.results: Regulated clients get self-service exploration without the deployment leaving their network.
axway.body:
## Air-gapped by requirement

Regulated environments frequently prohibit outbound connections entirely, which rules out most hosted analytics.

## What shipped

Out-of-the-box dashboards plus the ability for clients to explore, all within their own perimeter.

bdeo.challenge: Each team kept its own view of performance, and the numbers did not reconcile.
bdeo.solution: Shared models over the core data, with team-specific dashboards built on the same definitions.
bdeo.results: Teams work from one set of definitions, and cross-team reporting agrees.
bdeo.body:
## Reconciliation first

The work was less about dashboards than about settling which definition of each metric was correct.

## Afterwards

Teams build their own reporting on top, which is sustainable in a way that a central reporting queue is not.

billing-saas.challenge: Customers wanted analytics on their own billing activity, and building a reporting interface in-house would have taken a quarter.
billing-saas.solution: Embedded dashboards inside the platform, scoped per customer account.
billing-saas.results: Analytics shipped as a product feature without diverting the engineering roadmap.
billing-saas.body:
## Build or embed

Charting is the easy part. The query layer, permissions and caching are where the time goes.

## Scoping

Account identity comes from the signed token, and filtering happens at the data layer rather than in application code.

buena.challenge: Property management data was spread across systems with no shared reporting layer.
buena.solution: A consolidated model covering viewings, contracts and maintenance, delivered with an implementation partner.
buena.results: One place to answer operational questions, instead of three systems and a spreadsheet.
buena.body:
## Working with a partner

An external specialist handled the modelling, which is often faster than learning it while building it.

## What it enabled

Operational questions that previously required exporting from two systems now resolve in one view.

calcom.challenge: Answering product questions required engineering time, so most questions were not asked.
calcom.solution: Self-service analytics over product data, available to the whole team.
calcom.results: Non-engineers answer their own questions, and engineering time went back to the product.
calcom.body:
## The hidden cost

When a question costs an engineer an hour, people stop asking. The lost questions are invisible and are most of the cost.

## After

Support and product query directly. Engineering is involved when the model needs extending, not when someone needs a number.

cetec-erp.challenge: Manufacturing customers needed reporting inside the ERP, with each customer seeing only their own operation.
cetec-erp.solution: White-labelled embedded analytics with per-tenant data segregation.
cetec-erp.results: Enterprise-grade reporting shipped as part of the product rather than as a separate tool.
cetec-erp.body:
## Why white-label

Customers should not perceive reporting as a different product. Styling and navigation had to match.

## Isolation

Tenant scoping is enforced at the data layer, which is both safer and easier to demonstrate to a customer's auditor.

chromatic.challenge: Reporting relied on ad-hoc SQL written by a few people, so results were inconsistent and hard to share.
chromatic.solution: Shared, modelled analytics replacing the previous reporting tool, with self-serve exploration for the whole team.
chromatic.results: Analysis is shared and repeatable rather than re-derived each time someone needs it.
chromatic.body:
## The problem with ad-hoc

A query in someone's editor is not a shared asset. The next person rewrites it, slightly differently.

## What changed

Saved, named questions that others build on, which turns one person's analysis into something the team owns.

clockwise.challenge: Teams needed answers from product data but depended on a small group to get them.
clockwise.solution: Self-service analytics over modelled product events.
clockwise.results: Every team queries directly, and the data team supports the model rather than the queue.
clockwise.body:
## Scaling access

The constraint was never the data. It was how many people were able to ask it anything.

## The model layer

A well-named model covering core events removed most of the need for joins, which is what had been blocking non-specialists.

cypress.challenge: Decisions were being made without easy access to the data that should have informed them.
cypress.solution: Dashboards over product and usage data, accessible across the company.
cypress.results: Routine decisions now start from a number rather than a recollection.
cypress.body:
## Access changes behaviour

The measurable change was not better analysis. It was that people checked at all.

## Keeping it trustworthy

Ownership on each dashboard, so there is a person to ask when a number looks wrong.

dribbble.challenge: Data was available in principle and reachable by very few people in practice.
dribbble.solution: Company-wide self-service analytics over shared models.
dribbble.results: Teams across the business explore data directly rather than requesting extracts.
dribbble.body:
## Democratising access

The gap between having data and being able to use it is mostly tooling and permissions, not analytical skill.

## What made it work

Modelling the data so common questions did not require understanding the schema.

fabulous.challenge: Business reporting was assembled manually and inconsistently between weeks.
fabulous.solution: Automated reporting over shared models, with dashboards owned by the teams that use them.
fabulous.results: Reporting happens on schedule and does not depend on one person being available.
fabulous.body:
## Key-person risk

Several important numbers existed because one person remembered to update something. That is a reporting system in name only.

## Now

Scheduled, owned, and the same every week.

faros.challenge: Customers needed engineering operations reporting inside the product, across many tenants.
faros.solution: Embedded multi-tenant dashboards with isolation enforced at the data layer.
faros.results: Reporting became a product capability rather than a series of bespoke requests.
faros.body:
## Multi-tenant from the start

Designing for one customer and generalising later is how per-customer dashboards accumulate.

## Verification

Cross-tenant isolation is asserted in automated tests, because that failure is silent when it happens.

floryn.challenge: The existing BI setup was costly and difficult for non-specialists to use.
floryn.solution: A simpler analytics layer over the existing data, opened to every team.
floryn.results: Costs fell and more people are able to explore data without assistance.
floryn.body:
## Simplification as the goal

The previous tool was capable and nobody outside the data team could use it. Capability nobody can reach is not capability.

## Lending data

Loan book and risk reporting are now maintained by the teams that depend on them.

go-jek.challenge: Customer care operated at a scale where reporting had to be both company-wide and granular.
go-jek.solution: Shared analytics across customer care, with embedded views for operational teams.
go-jek.results: Transparency across a large operation, with teams able to drill into their own area.
go-jek.body:
## Scale changes the problem

At this size, one dashboard cannot serve everyone. The model has to support many views over consistent definitions.

## Consistency

Shared definitions were the prerequisite. Without them, every team's view disagrees with every other.

griffin-marine-services.challenge: Operational data lived in spreadsheets with no database behind it.
griffin-marine-services.solution: Uploading CSV data directly into the analytics layer, with reporting built on top.
griffin-marine-services.results: Reporting without a warehouse or a pipeline, which suited the size of the operation.
griffin-marine-services.body:
## Not every team needs a warehouse

For a team of this size, a pipeline would have been more machinery than the problem required.

## What they use

Direct CSV upload, modelled lightly, reported on consistently.

hola-health.challenge: Operational reporting was manual, so visibility lagged behind what was happening in the service.
hola-health.solution: Dashboards over appointment and clinician data, replacing the manual process.
hola-health.body:
## Latency was the issue

The reporting was accurate and arrived too late to act on, which is a familiar failure in operational settings.

## What shipped

Live views of appointments, utilisation and wait times, owned by the operations team.

hurb.challenge: Decision-making relied on reports that took time to produce and were not always current.
hurb.solution: Self-service dashboards over booking and customer data.
hurb.results: Faster decisions, with teams able to check rather than request.
hurb.body:
## Travel data moves quickly

In a business where pricing and demand shift daily, a weekly report is a historical document.

## The change

Teams look at current numbers themselves, and the reporting function supports the model rather than producing documents.

insocial.challenge: Generating customer-facing feedback dashboards required engineering effort for each new client.
insocial.solution: Embedded dashboards generated from a shared template, scoped per client.
insocial.results: A large amount of recurring engineering effort removed.
insocial.body:
## Per-client work does not scale

Every bespoke dashboard is a maintenance commitment that compounds with each new customer.

## The alternative

One dashboard, parameterised. New clients require configuration rather than engineering.

klog.challenge: Freight customers wanted shipment reporting, and operations produced it by hand.
klog.solution: Embedded dashboards in the customer portal covering shipment status and exceptions.
klog.results: Customers self-serve, and the manual reporting run was retired.
klog.body:
## The weekly run

Manually assembled customer reports are stale on arrival and consume operational capacity every week.

## What customers get

Status and exceptions as they happen, which turned out to matter more than the hours saved.

kula-project.challenge: Programme outcomes needed reporting to funders, with limited capacity to produce it.
kula-project.solution: Shared models over programme data, with dashboards per reporting requirement.
kula-project.results: Funder reporting is produced on schedule without consuming programme capacity.
kula-project.body:
## Capacity is the constraint

For a small organisation, every hour on compliance reporting is an hour not spent on the programme.

## Working with a partner

An implementation partner handled setup, which is often the difference between a project happening and not.

lime-technologies.challenge: CRM customers wanted analytics on their own data, branded as part of the product.
lime-technologies.solution: White-labelled embedded analytics within the CRM.
lime-technologies.results: Customers answer their own questions inside the product they already use.
lime-technologies.body:
## Branding matters

Analytics that looks like a different product undermines the impression that it is part of the one you sold.

## Scope

Each customer sees only their own data, enforced below the application layer.

linstol.challenge: Reporting across a distribution business was fragmented and slow to produce.
linstol.solution: Consolidated analytics over sales and inventory data, delivered with a partner.
linstol.results: A single view of the business, maintained by the teams that use it.
linstol.body:
## Consolidation

The difficulty was less technical than definitional: agreeing what a sale, a return and a unit meant across regions.

## Outcome

One model, several team-specific views built on it.

marketfuel.challenge: In-app reporting was a customer requirement, and a from-scratch build would have delayed the roadmap.
marketfuel.solution: Embedded analytics against existing data, with no new pipeline.
marketfuel.results: A working proof of concept very quickly, which de-risked the decision.
marketfuel.body:
## Proof of concept first

The value of getting to a prototype quickly is that it converts an architectural argument into something people can look at.

## What followed

The prototype became the shipped feature with styling and scoping work, not a rewrite.

matter.challenge: Growth spending decisions were made without clear visibility of which channels produced lasting users.
matter.solution: Analytics joining acquisition data to product engagement.
matter.results: A meaningful share of growth budget redirected away from channels that were not working.
matter.body:
## Volume is not quality

Channels with identical cost per signup can have completely different activation rates, and spend reports hide that entirely.

## The join

Connecting acquisition source to downstream engagement is the whole exercise.

myagro.challenge: Field programme data needed to be usable by teams without analytical training.
myagro.solution: Modelled data with dashboards designed for non-specialists.
myagro.results: Field and programme teams answer their own questions.
myagro.body:
## Designing for the reader

When the audience has no analytical background, the modelling has to do more work so the interface can do less.

## What that meant

Fewer tables, clearer names, and defaults that are correct without configuration.

n26.challenge: A fast-growing bank needed analytics accessible beyond the data team while meeting regulatory expectations.
n26.solution: Governed self-service analytics with permissions mapped to existing groups.
n26.body:
## Governance and access together

In a regulated setting these are usually traded against each other. They do not have to be, if permissions are modelled rather than managed by hand.

## Groups, not individuals

Mapping to existing identity groups keeps access correct as people move teams.

onecom.challenge: Reporting was needed both internally and for managed-service customers.
onecom.solution: Internal dashboards plus embedded customer-facing reporting from the same models.
onecom.results: One model serving two audiences, rather than two parallel reporting stacks.
onecom.body:
## Shared foundations

Internal and customer-facing reporting usually diverge into separate systems. Building both on one model avoids the divergence.

## The constraint

Customer-facing views need stricter scoping, which is a permissions problem rather than a modelling one.

onepark.challenge: Booking and operational data was not easily accessible to the teams who needed it.
onepark.results: Operational teams track performance without requesting reports.
onepark.body:
## Removing the request step

Most operational questions are simple and frequent, which is exactly the category that should never require a ticket.

## Afterwards

The analytics function works on the model rather than on requests.

owlery.challenge: Manufacturers and brands needed visibility into their own logistics data inside the platform.
owlery.results: Customers see their own operation without an export or a request.
owlery.body:
## Why embedded

Logistics customers check frequently and briefly. A monthly export does not fit that pattern.

## Scoping

Account identity travels with the session, and filtering happens below the application.

recruit-crm.challenge: Recruitment agencies using the product wanted reporting on their own pipelines.
recruit-crm.solution: Embedded dashboards inside the applicant tracking product.
recruit-crm.results: Reporting became part of the product rather than a request queue.
recruit-crm.body:
## Customer-facing from the start

Agencies compare their own performance over time, which requires history and consistency more than it requires flexibility.

## Implementation

One parameterised dashboard rather than per-agency builds.

reforge.challenge: Understanding how learners engaged with programmes required data the team could not easily reach.
reforge.solution: Self-service analytics over programme and engagement data.
reforge.results: Programme decisions are informed by engagement data rather than assumption.
reforge.body:
## Engagement over completion

Completion rates are easy and misleading. Engagement patterns during a programme are the more useful signal.

## Access

Programme staff query directly rather than requesting analysis.

retargetly.challenge: A data platform business needed internal analytics that could keep up with its own data volume.
retargetly.solution: Analytics over the existing warehouse with modelled, reusable definitions.
retargetly.results: Internal teams work from consistent definitions at scale.
retargetly.body:
## Practising what you sell

Data companies are not automatically good at their own internal analytics, and often worse because everything looks solvable.

## What helped

Treating internal definitions with the same rigour as customer-facing ones.

sincera.challenge: Customers needed access to verification data in a form they could explore themselves.
sincera.solution: Embedded analytics over the verification dataset, scoped per customer.
sincera.results: Customers investigate their own data instead of requesting extracts.
sincera.body:
## Exploration, not reports

When customers' questions are open-ended, a fixed report generates follow-up requests indefinitely.

## The approach

Give them the ability to filter and drill within their own scope.

spocket.challenge: A marketplace connecting two sides needed reporting that reflected both.
spocket.solution: Shared models covering supplier and retailer activity, with dashboards per team.
spocket.results: Teams see both sides of the marketplace from consistent definitions.
spocket.body:
## Two-sided reporting

Marketplace metrics are easy to state and hard to define: an active supplier and an active retailer are different things measured differently.

## Definitions

Settling those was the bulk of the work and the bulk of the value.

sunglass-fix.challenge: A small team needed reporting without the overhead of a data function.
sunglass-fix.solution: Lightweight analytics over existing order data.
sunglass-fix.results: Reporting proportionate to the size of the business.
sunglass-fix.body:
## Right-sizing

Small businesses are frequently sold infrastructure designed for much larger ones.

## What this looks like

A handful of dashboards over the operational database, maintained by the people who use them.

synctera.challenge: Banking platform customers required analytics with strict separation between them.
synctera.solution: Embedded analytics with per-tenant isolation and curated, vetted content.
synctera.results: Customers explore their own data within boundaries that satisfy compliance review.
synctera.body:
## Marking what is trustworthy

Distinguishing vetted content from exploratory work tells people where to start, which matters more as the volume grows.

## Isolation

Enforced at the data layer and demonstrable, which is what a compliance review actually asks for.

treebo.challenge: A franchise hotel operation needed consistent reporting across independently run properties.
treebo.results: Properties and head office work from the same definitions.
treebo.body:
## Franchise reporting

The difficulty is that each property operates independently but has to be comparable.

## Shared definitions

Occupancy and revenue per room defined once centrally, reported per property.

uptime.challenge: Service providers needed visibility into equipment status across many installations.
uptime.solution: Analytics over device and service data, with reporting for service teams.
uptime.results: Issues are visible earlier, which shortens response time.
uptime.body:
## Connected equipment

Device telemetry is high volume and mostly uninteresting. The value is in surfacing the small fraction that is not.

## What is reported

Status, exceptions and service history, aggregated to the level a service team can act on.

usabilla.challenge: Feedback data was collected at volume but was hard to analyse across customers and time.
usabilla.solution: Modelled analytics over qualitative and quantitative feedback.
usabilla.results: Trends are visible across the dataset rather than per response.
usabilla.body:
## Qualitative at scale

Individual feedback is readable; thousands of responses need categorisation before any of it is analysable.

## The modelling

Categorising by underlying theme rather than by the form field the respondent selected.

yellowcard.challenge: A rapidly growing fintech needed analytics accessible across a large, distributed team.
yellowcard.solution: Self-serve analytics over governed models, with permissions mapped to existing groups.
yellowcard.results: Analytics scaled across the organisation without a corresponding increase in the data team.
yellowcard.body:
## Scaling access, not headcount

The alternative to self-service is hiring analysts in proportion to questions, which does not work.

## Governance

Curated models and clear ownership, so wider access did not mean inconsistent answers.
